title: A Response, a Rebuttal, and an Ongoing Conversation About Reading Recovery
author: Jen O'Sullivan
summary: O'Sullivan responds publicly to Reading Recovery Europe's counter-argument to her peer-reviewed article questioning Reading Recovery's place in Irish national policy. She identifies four structural problems in RRE's rebuttal: it attacks a straw-man position she never advanced (that absence of evaluation equals failure) rather than her narrower methodological claim; it uses quotation marks that do not match her actual wording, compromising readers' ability to evaluate the critique; it fails to engage with the core instructional-design critique — whether phonics is delivered explicitly, systematically, and cumulatively enough for children with persistent word reading difficulties, not merely whether phonics appears in the program; and it applies contextual-specificity arguments selectively, discounting U.S. studies while accepting UK findings without equivalent scrutiny. O'Sullivan makes the exchange visible by sharing all three documents — her original article link, the RRE PDF, and her rebuttal — as a model of transparent professional dialogue. Her underlying argument is simple: when an intervention sits at the heart of national policy for the most vulnerable young readers, it is reasonable to ask whether it still reflects the best available evidence.
points: RRE's response argues against a position O'Sullivan never made — that absence of national evaluation means failure — rather than engaging with her actual argument that contextual effectiveness claims are constrained without independent Irish data.

Academic quotation marks in RRE's response do not always match O'Sullivan's wording; this is not a minor presentational issue because precise attribution is the mechanism by which readers evaluate the accuracy of a critique.

The most important unanswered question is whether Reading Recovery's phonics instruction is sufficiently explicit, systematic, and cumulative for children with persistent word reading difficulties — reported gains on phonics measures do not resolve whether the instructional design meets those children's specific needs.

Contextual-specificity arguments must be applied consistently; discounting U.S. findings while accepting UK findings without equal scrutiny is a methodological inconsistency that undermines the entire principle being invoked.
O'Sullivan models the norm she advocates: making the full exchange publicly visible so readers can assess the arguments themselves rather than depend on organizational narratives.
quotes: One of the features of the RRE response is the way in which my original argument is characterised. At several points, the RRE response reads the article as asserting that the absence of a national Irish evaluation indicates that RR has failed. It then devotes considerable attention to demonstrating that a lack of evaluation data is not evidence of failure. However, that is not the position advanced in the article.

In several instances, phrases are presented in quotation marks in a manner that suggests they are drawn directly from the article. In a number of cases, these do not correspond to the wording used in the article, and, in some cases, were not mentioned at all. This is not a minor presentational issue. In academic discourse, quotation marks signal precise attribution.

The question is not whether phonics is included, but whether it is delivered in a sufficiently explicit, systematic, and cumulative way to meet the needs of children with persistent word reading difficulties. As a result, while reported gains are important, they do not in themselves resolve questions about alignment between instructional approach and current theoretical models of reading development.

If contextual specificity is to function as an analytical principle, it must be applied systematically across the evidence base. It cannot operate selectively, whereby findings from one context are discounted on the grounds of difference, while findings from another are accepted without equivalent scrutiny.

Literacy policy decisions are rarely straightforward. They involve questions of evidence, resources, instructional design, and long-term impact, all of which carry real consequences for children’s learning. Where there are different interpretations of that evidence, it is important that those differences are open to scrutiny rather than settled behind closed doors or reduced to simplified narratives.

When an intervention sits at the heart of national policy, particularly one aimed at young children with the most persistent reading difficulties, it is reasonable to ask whether it continues to reflect the best available evidence and represents the most effective use of limited resources.
